mcqs.question: Why do languages built around immutability, like Haskell or Erlang, lean on recursion instead of a mutable-counter for loop as their default repetition construct?
options: Recursion is always faster than a for loop on any hardware
Their compilers cannot generate machine code for loop constructs
For loops require a garbage collector, which these languages don't have
A for loop's counter is mutable state being updated every iteration, which conflicts with the language's immutability discipline; recursion instead passes new values as fresh arguments
mcqs.explanation: A mutable loop counter is exactly the kind of in-place state change these languages avoid; recursion achieves repetition by passing new, immutable argument values to each call instead. Performance and compiler capability aren't the reason, and the garbage-collector claim is false — several of these languages do use one.

mcqs.question: return n * factorial(n - 1) is not tail-recursive. What specifically disqualifies it from tail position?
options: It disqualifies because factorial is recursive at all — no recursive call can be in tail position
It disqualifies because the base case uses a different return statement than the recursive case
There's pending work (the multiplication by n) that must happen after the recursive call returns, so the call isn't the last action taken
It disqualifies because n is passed by value instead of by reference
mcqs.explanation: Tail position requires the recursive call to be the very last action, with nothing left to do afterward. Here, multiplying by n happens after factorial(n-1) returns, which is exactly the pending work that blocks tail position. Recursion itself isn't disqualifying, and neither passing convention nor differing base-case syntax is relevant.

mcqs.question: Mechanically, what does a compiler do differently for a tail call compared to an ordinary recursive call?
options: It overwrites the current stack frame with the new call's arguments and jumps, instead of pushing a new frame on top
It converts the function into a different, non-recursive algorithm automatically
It runs the tail call on a separate thread to avoid stack growth
It caches the result of every call so repeated calls are skipped
mcqs.explanation: Because a tail call leaves nothing for the current frame's locals to do afterward, the compiler can safely reuse that frame's space for the new call instead of allocating a fresh one — the same shape as a backward jump in a while loop. It isn't multithreading, algorithm substitution, or memoization.

mcqs.question: A candidate writes tail-recursive JavaScript intended to run in Node/V8 and assumes it's now safe on unbounded input because tail calls are in the ES2015 spec. What's wrong with that assumption?
options: Nothing — ES2015 tail calls are guaranteed to work in every JavaScript engine
Being in the language specification doesn't guarantee the runtime implements it; V8 and most engines never shipped proper tail calls, so deep recursion still overflows in practice
Tail calls only apply to arrow functions, not regular function declarations
The rewrite is wrong because JavaScript doesn't support recursion at all
mcqs.explanation: Tail position is necessary but not sufficient for TCO — the runtime must actually implement the optimization, and V8 (which Node and Chrome use) never shipped it despite it being specified. JavaScript fully supports recursion generally, and the gap isn't about function syntax.

mcqs.question: Before relying on tail-call optimization to avoid a stack overflow on large input, what should you actually verify?
options: That the function has at least one base case
That the recursive call is syntactically the last line of the function, which alone guarantees safety
That the specific runtime/engine version you're deploying to actually implements TCO, not just that the language spec allows it
That the input is sorted before recursing
mcqs.explanation: Tail position (being the last action) is necessary but not sufficient; the concrete runtime has to actually perform the frame-reuse optimization, which varies by engine and version — JavaScript's V8 is the textbook counter-example. A base case is required for correctness but doesn't address stack growth, and sort order is unrelated.

mcqs.question: In the trampoline pattern, why does factorial_thunk returning a lambda instead of calling itself directly avoid stack growth?
options: Because lambdas execute on a separate call stack from regular functions
Because returning a thunk means the current call finishes and returns immediately, so no frame needs to wait on a nested call — the driver loop does the repeated work at one constant stack depth
Because the Python interpreter automatically detects thunks and applies TCO to them
Because lambdas in Python are always evaluated lazily and therefore use no stack space
mcqs.explanation: Returning a thunk lets the current call return right away instead of waiting on a nested call's result, so nothing needs to stay on the stack — the trampoline's while loop then invokes each returned thunk in turn, all at the same stack depth. Python has no special-case TCO detection, and this has nothing to do with separate stacks or lazy evaluation.
